passages.t: Through Macedonia and Greece, with the gift for Jerusalem
passages.happening:
When the uproar ends, Paul sends for the disciples, encourages them, says goodbye and leaves for Macedonia (verse 1). He travels through that area, speaking many words of encouragement, and comes to Greece (verse 2), where he stays three months. When a plot is made against him as he is about to sail for Syria, he decides to go back through Macedonia (verse 3).

With him go Sopater from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia (verse 4). They go ahead and wait for ‘us’ at Troas (verse 5). After the Feast of Unleavened Bread, ‘we’ sail from Philippi and reach Troas five days later, and stay seven days (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Luke covers many months in a few lines. Paul's letters fill in some of the story. From Macedonia he probably wrote to the Corinthians again, and ‘Greece’ here means mainly Corinth, where many think he wrote his letter to the Romans during these three months.

Verse 3 says ‘the Jews formed a plot against him’. Luke means some opponents in Greece who planned to attack Paul as he sailed, not the Jewish people. The note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads Luke's ‘the Jews’, and the note on 2:22-28 why such verses must never be turned against the Jewish people.

Look at the list of names in verse 4. They come from the churches Paul had planted: Macedonia, Galatia, Asia. Many scholars think these men were carrying a gift. Paul's letters speak of a collection he gathered from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem: ‘Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem’ (Romans 15:26). He had asked the churches to send their own trusted people with it (1 Corinthians 16:3). Acts mentions the gift only later, in passing (24:17).

That gift said something. Gentile churches were sending help to the Jewish believers in Jerusalem, the mother church. Paul wanted the two to know they were one family.

And the ‘we’ returns. It had stopped at Philippi in chapter 16. Now it picks up again at Philippi. The writer is travelling with Paul once more.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread was the week of Passover, in the spring. Paul still kept the Jewish calendar.
passages.ot:
The gift for Jerusalem fits the Law's command to care for the poor: “Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so” (Deuteronomy 15:10). And the nations bringing gifts to Jerusalem was a picture the prophets loved: “the wealth of the nations will come to you” (Isaiah 60:5).

The Feast of Unleavened Bread remembered Israel's hurried escape from Egypt, when there was no time for the bread to rise (Exodus 12:39).
passages.asks: Gentile churches gave to poor Jewish believers they had never met, and sent trusted people to carry it honestly. Ask whom your giving reaches beyond your own circle. And notice the care: many hands, chosen by the churches, so that no one could say the money went astray. Ask whether your church handles money in a way no one could question.

passages.happening:
“On the first day of the week we came together to break bread” (verse 7). Since Paul is leaving the next day, he talks to them until midnight. There are many lamps in the upper room where they are gathered (verse 8).

A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sinks into a deep sleep as Paul talks on and on. Sound asleep, he falls from the third storey “and was picked up dead” (verse 9). Paul goes down, throws himself on the young man and puts his arms around him. “Do not be alarmed!” he says. “He is still alive!” (verse 10).

Paul goes back upstairs, breaks bread and eats, and keeps talking until daybreak; then he leaves (verse 11). And the people are greatly relieved to take the boy home alive (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The believers meet ‘on the first day of the week’, Sunday, the day Jesus rose. They meet to ‘break bread’, which in Acts means sharing a meal together, very likely including the Lord's Supper.

They meet in the evening. In the Roman world Sunday was an ordinary working day, so believers, many of them slaves and labourers, could only gather after work. Which evening is meant is read in two ways. By Jewish reckoning a day began at sunset, so ‘the first day’ could have begun on Saturday evening. By Roman reckoning it would be Sunday evening.

An upper room on the third storey suggests a crowded city building. Many lamps, a warm room full of people, a long talk late at night: it is not hard to see why a young man sitting in an open window fell asleep. ‘Young man’ may mean a teenager; in verse 12 he is called ‘the boy’.

Luke says he was ‘picked up dead’. Paul goes down and throws himself on him, as Elijah and Elisha did over dead children. Most readers take the story as a raising from the dead. Some think Paul's words, ‘He is still alive’, mean that he found life still in him. Luke's own words, ‘picked up dead’, point to the first reading.

And then, remarkably, they all go back upstairs, eat together, and keep talking until dawn.
passages.ot:
Paul throwing himself on the boy recalls two prophets. Elijah “stretched himself out over the child three times and cried out to the LORD” (1 Kings 17:21), and the boy lived. Elisha “got on the bed and lay on the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, and hand to hand” (2 Kings 4:34), and the boy's body became warm.

The Law had given Israel the seventh day, the Sabbath, as a day of rest: “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:8).
passages.hard:
Does this verse show that Christians should worship on Sunday? It is one of the earliest signs in the New Testament of believers gathering on the first day of the week, along with Paul's instruction to set aside money ‘on the first day of every week’ (1 Corinthians 16:2). Early Christian writings outside the Bible, such as a teaching handbook called the Didache and the writer Justin Martyr in the second century, speak of Christians meeting on the Lord's day, the day of the resurrection. Most churches gather on Sunday for that reason.

Some Christians, such as Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists, keep Saturday, the seventh day, as the Sabbath, and hold that verses like this one describe a meeting, not a change of the Sabbath commandment. Others hold that Christians are free in the matter (Romans 14:5-6). These notes do not choose between these views. All agree that the risen Lord is the reason his people gather.
passages.asks: The believers at Troas met after a long day's work, ate together, and stayed up all night to learn. Ask how much the gathering of God's people means to you. And notice how Luke ends: the church took a young man home alive and was ‘greatly relieved’. The church was a family that noticed who was missing and carried him home.

passages.happening:
The others go ahead to the ship and sail to Assos, where they are to take Paul aboard; he has chosen to go there on foot (verse 13). At Assos they take him aboard and go on to Mitylene (verse 14). From there they sail past Chios, on to Samos, and the next day to Miletus (verse 15).

Paul has decided to sail past Ephesus, so as not to spend time in the province of Asia, “because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
These verses read like a ship's log: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos, Miletus, small ports and islands along the coast of what is now western Turkey. Ships of the time kept close to the coast, stopping each night. The ‘we’ shows that the writer was on board.

Why did Paul walk to Assos while the others sailed? Luke does not say. Perhaps he wanted time alone, or time with friends along the road.

Pentecost was a Jewish feast fifty days after Passover, when Jewish pilgrims from many lands came to Jerusalem. Paul wants to be there for it, with the gift from the Gentile churches. If he stopped in Ephesus, where he had spent three years and had so many friends, he would be held up for days. So he sails past, and sends for the leaders to meet him at Miletus instead.
passages.ot:
Pentecost was the Law's Feast of Weeks, a harvest feast: “You are to count off seven weeks from the time you first put the sickle to the standing grain” (Deuteronomy 16:9). On that feast the Spirit had first come on the church (Acts 2:1).

Paul's haste to reach Jerusalem for a feast follows the Law's call for Israel to go up to the LORD's chosen place at the great feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16).
passages.asks: Paul sailed past a city full of friends because he had a task to finish. Ask whether there are good things you need to pass by so that you can do what you have been given to do. And notice that he did not simply ignore his friends. He sent for them. Ask how you can keep faith with people even when you cannot stay.

passages.t: Paul's farewell: how he lived among them
passages.happening:
From Miletus, Paul sends to Ephesus for the elders of the church (verse 17). When they come, he says, “You know how I lived the whole time I was with you, from the first day I arrived in the province of Asia” (verse 18). He served the Lord with great humility and with tears, through the trials that came on him through plots against him (verse 19). He did not hold back anything helpful, teaching publicly and from house to house (verse 20), urging Jews and Greeks alike to turn to God and to have faith in the Lord Jesus (verse 21).

“And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there” (verse 22). In town after town the Holy Spirit warns him that chains and afflictions are waiting (verse 23). But he considers his life of no value to himself, if only he may finish his course and complete the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus, telling the good news of God's grace (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to believers, to church leaders he had trained. Many readers hear in it the speech in Acts that sounds most like Paul's own letters: serving with humility, tears, working with his hands, finishing the race, the grace of God.

Miletus was a port to the south of Ephesus, so the elders had to come some distance.

Paul begins with how he lived. ‘You know.’ He can point to his own life because they had watched it for three years. Humility, tears, trials. Teaching ‘publicly and from house to house’, in the lecture hall and in homes. Holding nothing back.

Verse 19 speaks of ‘the plots of the Jews’. Luke means opponents in Ephesus and elsewhere who plotted against Paul, not the Jewish people; the same verse goes on to say that Paul preached to ‘Jews and Greeks alike’, and he was himself a Jew. The note on Acts 13:42-47 says more.

Then he looks ahead. He is going to Jerusalem, ‘compelled by the Spirit’, and the Spirit keeps warning him that prison and suffering wait there. He goes anyway. His life is not the thing he values most. Finishing the work Jesus gave him is.
passages.ot:
Paul's look back on his life is like Samuel's farewell to Israel: “Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed?” (1 Samuel 12:3). Both men could ask their people to bear witness to how they had lived.

His readiness to go where suffering waits echoes the prophets, who were sent knowing they would be resisted. God told Ezekiel to speak his words to Israel “whether they listen or refuse to listen” (Ezekiel 2:7).
passages.asks: Paul could say, ‘You know how I lived.’ Ask whether the people who know you best could say the same of your faith. And ask what you value more than your own comfort. Paul's answer was finishing the task Jesus gave him. What is yours?

passages.t: ‘Be shepherds of the church of God’
passages.happening:
Paul tells them that none of them will see his face again (verse 25). So he declares that he is “innocent of the blood of all men” (verse 26), for he has not held back from declaring the whole will of God (verse 27).

“Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood” (verse 28). After he leaves, “savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock” (verse 29). Even from among themselves men will rise up and twist the truth to draw disciples after them (verse 30). So they must be alert, and remember that for three years he never stopped warning each of them, night and day, with tears (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
‘Innocent of the blood of all men’ is the watchman's language again, as in Corinth (18:6): Paul has given the warning, and he has done his part.

Notice the words he uses for these leaders. Luke calls them ‘elders’ (verse 17). Paul says the Holy Spirit has made them ‘overseers’ (verse 28); the Greek word, episkopoi, is the word from which English gets ‘bishop’ and ‘episcopal’. And he tells them to ‘be shepherds’, which is what ‘pastor’ means. Here the three words describe the same group of men. Many readers agree that at this early stage ‘elder’ and ‘overseer’ named the same people (compare Titus 1:5-7).

Churches today read this in different ways, as the note on Acts 14:21-28 sets out. Some churches are led by bishops with priests or pastors under them, as in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches; they hold that the office of bishop grew from the apostles and their helpers, and early in the second century letters of Ignatius of Antioch already speak of one bishop in each city with elders and deacons. Some are led by a group of elders together, as in Presbyterian churches, and point to this chapter's many elders. Some are governed by their members, as in Baptist and many other churches. These notes do not choose between them. All agree on what Paul asks of leaders: watch yourselves first, then feed and guard the flock.

‘The church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.’ This is a striking phrase, since God is spirit. Some early copies read ‘the church of the Lord’; most modern Bibles, the Berean Standard Bible among them, read ‘the church of God’. The Greek can also be read ‘with the blood of His own’, meaning his own Son, and some translations put it that way. On either reading, the church was bought at the cost of Christ's death, and that was God's own act.

‘Savage wolves.’ Paul warns of danger from outside, teachers who would harm the believers, and, harder still, from inside: men from their own number who would twist the truth to gather followers for themselves. He does not name anyone. He tells the leaders to stay awake.
passages.ot:
The picture of leaders as shepherds runs through the Old Testament. “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). And God condemned shepherds who used the flock: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). The wolves have their picture too: Ezekiel said Jerusalem's officials were “like wolves tearing their prey” (Ezekiel 22:27).

The watchman who is innocent of blood once he has given warning is God's word to Ezekiel: “if you warn a wicked man and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself” (Ezekiel 3:19).
passages.asks: Paul told leaders to watch over themselves first, and then the flock. If you lead anyone, a church, a group, a family, ask whether you are watching your own life. And ask whether you would notice a wolf: someone who twists the truth to draw people after himself. Such people may speak from the front of a church.

passages.t: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’
passages.happening:
“And now I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified” (verse 32). Paul has not wanted anyone's silver, gold or clothing (verse 33). “You yourselves know that these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions” (verse 34). By hard work like this, he says, we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’ (verse 35).

Then Paul kneels down with all of them and prays (verse 36). They all weep openly as they embrace and kiss him (verse 37). What grieves them most is that they will never see his face again. Then they go with him to the ship (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not leave the elders a program. He leaves them to God, and to ‘the word of His grace’, which can build them up.

He holds up his hands, work-hardened hands, as his last lesson. In the Greek world travelling teachers were often suspected of living off their followers. Paul had made tents and paid his own way, and he had used what he earned to help others too. The point is not that leaders must never be paid; Paul says elsewhere that those who preach the gospel may live by it (1 Corinthians 9:14). The point is that the weak come first.

Then he quotes Jesus: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ These words are not found in any of the four Gospels. The early church remembered sayings of Jesus that were not all written down in them, and here Paul, or Luke, preserves one. Its meaning is simple and deep: the giver is the one who is truly rich.

The ending is one of the most human scenes in Acts. Grown men kneel on a beach, pray, weep, embrace and kiss their friend goodbye. Faith did not make them stiff or cold. It made them love one another.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knew the blessing of giving: “One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor” (Proverbs 11:24), and “he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed” (Proverbs 11:25).

Paul's commitment of the elders to God echoes the farewells of Israel's leaders. Before he died, Moses blessed the people, and Joshua gathered the elders and leaders of Israel to charge them to keep faith with the LORD (Joshua 23:2).
passages.asks: Paul's last lesson was his own hands, used to help the weak, and a saying of Jesus: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Ask whether you believe that, really, in your spending and your time. And look at the farewell on the beach. Ask whom you love like that, and whether they know it.
